heading: Step 4: Call the server from the page
body:
This step is shown in JavaScript, TypeScript, Dart, C#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby and C++. Dart, C#, Rust, Go, Kotlin, Swift, Java, Ruby and C++ use the default same-origin browser transport, which waits without blocking the page (ADR 0090). Lua has no tab here, because the build refuses HTTPClient in Lua Tac code with TY1308. Python has no example here yet. F# has the browser transport, but it does not inject an HTTPClient yet: an F# service makes its own BehaviorContext and asks its REST client, as the F# section of Calling the server from a page shows. A client class sends HTTP requests for the page. Put it in `client/remotes`. `HTTPClient` marks the class. `GetRequest("/api/greeting")` makes the method `getGreeting` send a GET request to the controller of step 3. Leave the method body empty: Tachyon writes it. An empty body returns nothing to the type checker, so the method declares its answer as `Promise<Greeting | void>`. `export default` lets the type checker and the other classes find the client without an import.

In Dart, the client is an abstract interface whose method declares `Future<Greeting>`. Leave the declaration without a body: Tachyon generates the method and reads the typed model after the request completes. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the default transport handles this relative URL; a matching configured custom adapter still takes precedence. The browser remains responsive while the Future is pending. Credentials are omitted, including same-origin cookies. This default transport refuses other origins; the Dart example does not promise the separate outgoing-host support of other adapters.

In the service, `Needs` asks Tachyon to put a `GreetingClient` into the field `greetingClient`. The method `askServer` waits for the answer. The private method `messageOf` gives its message, or an empty text when there is no answer, and `askServer` saves it in the field `message`. A public method of a service holds no decision (TY1314), so the check sits in the private method. The page has its own copy of the model in `client/models/Greeting.ts`, because the browser cannot read files in `server/`. JavaScript reads its type with `/** @import { Greeting } from '/models/Greeting.ts' */`. Change the component, the service and add the client. The page file stays the same as in step 2.

Dart has its own `client/models/Greeting.dart`. Its immutable injected `GreetingClient` is created by Tachyon; the service does not construct a client or call fetch. `Future<void> askServer()` awaits the typed answer and saves its message. Step 5 uses a typed Fake field and `construct<CounterService>(CounterService)` to test this same HTTP-enabled service. The test constructs its generated `GreetingClient` with its own BehaviorContext, whose HelloTestSetup supplies a custom HTTP adapter. The awaited test checks typed decoding and the saved message without calling the server.

In C#, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient`. Its generated `getGreeting()` returns `Task<Models.Greeting>`. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the same-origin browser transport handles the request and omits cookies and authorization. The service receives a private readonly client through `Needs`; it does not construct one or use browser APIs. Its public `AskServer()` coordinates the request, and its private `_accept` method awaits the typed answer and saves the message. This example uses a registered scalar record; it does not promise arbitrary or nested Task result models. Step 5 supplies a typed Fake client with a caller-owned BehaviorContext and tests the same service without a network request.

In Rust, `GreetingClient` is a trait marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method is `async fn get_greeting(&self) -> BehaviorResult<Greeting>;` without a body: Tachyon writes it, sends the request, and reads the answer into the `Greeting` model of `client/models/Greeting.rs`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `BehaviorConfiguration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `#[Needs]` above `greeting_client: std::sync::Arc<GreetingClient>` asks Tachyon for the client; the other fields start empty. The service has no `fn new` now, because Tachyon builds it. `pub async fn ask_server(&mut self) -> BehaviorResult<()>` awaits the answer with `.await`, and `?` passes an error, such as `HTTP_STATUS`, back to the page. While `ask_server` waits, the page keeps working and shows the fields as they were; a click on Click me runs after the answer.

In Go, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `// @HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `GetGreeting() (Greeting, error)` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` model of `client/models/Greeting.go`, with its `json` tags. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty configuration, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `// @Needs` above `greetingClient *GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `AskServer` calls it like any Go function and returns its error. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own goroutine: while `AskServer` waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns.

In Kotlin, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `suspend fun getGreeting(): Greeting` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` data class of `client/models/Greeting.kt`, which the client imports with `import models.Greeting`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `Behaviors.Configuration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private val greetingClient: GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `suspend fun askServer()` calls the client like any other function. While it waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `Behaviors.Failure` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Swift, `GreetingClient` is a protocol marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `func getGreeting() async throws -> Greeting` has no body: Tachyon writes it and decodes the answer into the `Codable` struct `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.swift`. `GreetingSetup` returns empty `BehaviorAdapters`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private let greetingClient: GreetingClient` asks Tachyon for the client. `func askServer() async throws` calls the client with `try await`. While it waits for the answer, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `BehaviorError` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Java, `GreetingClient` is an interface marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `Greeting getGreeting();` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the record `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.java`, which the client imports with `import models.Greeting;`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty `Behaviors.Configuration`, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `@Needs` above `private final GreetingClient greetingClient;` asks Tachyon for the client. `void askServer()` calls the client like any other method; Java has no async keyword. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own TeaVM fiber: when the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once, as before. When it waits for the server, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request throws a `Behaviors.Failure` whose `code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In Ruby, `GreetingClient` is a class marked with `HTTPClient("/api")`. Its method `get_greeting` has an empty body: Tachyon writes it. The comment `# @return [Greeting]` above it tells Tachyon to read the answer into the model `Greeting` of `client/models/Greeting.rb`. `GreetingSetup` returns an empty Hash, so the browser transport sends the request to the same origin and leaves out cookies. In the service, `#[Needs]` above `attr_reader :greeting_client`, with `# @return [GreetingClient]` between them, asks Tachyon for the client, and the service calls it as `greeting_client`. `ask_server` calls the client like any other method; Ruby has no async keyword. Tachyon runs each call of a service method in its own Ruby fiber: when the method does not wait, the page gets its answer at once, as before. When it waits for the server, the page keeps working, and the page gets a promise that settles when the method returns. A failed request raises a `BehaviorError` whose `behavior_code` names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

In C++, `GreetingClient` is a class marked with `[[HTTPClient("/api")]]` in `client/remotes/GreetingClient.hpp`. Its method `Task<Greeting> getGreeting();` has no body: Tachyon writes it and reads the answer into the `Greeting` struct of `client/models/Greeting.hpp`. C++ needs no Setup, because every C++ request goes through the browser transport to the same origin, without cookies. In the service, `[[Needs]] GreetingClient& greetingClient;` asks Tachyon for the client. `Task<void> askServer()` waits for the answer with `co_await`, and the page gets a promise that settles when the task ends. A failed request throws an `HttpRequestException` whose code names the problem, such as `HTTP_STATUS`.

Result: click Ask the server. The text Hello from Yon appears under the buttons. A path such as `/api/greeting` stays on the same origin, so no host needs to be listed. For adapters that support requests to another host, that host must be listed in `tac.outgoing.hosts`; the current Dart default transport remains same-origin only.
